10.1002/adem.71392.abstract: Mixed antimony chalcogenides (Sb 2 E 3 , E = S, Se) as solar light absorbers offer bandgap tunability with favorable optical and electrical properties. However, depositing continuous films of thickness adjusted to the high optical absorption coefficients (<100 nm) has been challenging due to the favored formation of crystalline needles. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) as an ideally conformal deposition method is suited to addressing this challenge, but in the case of Sb 2 Se 3 , nucleation chemistry effects can render the substrate inert. Using tris(dimethylamido)antimony (Sb(NMe 2 ) 3 ) and bis(trimethylsilyl)selenide ((Me 3 Si) 2 Se) as precursors, we demonstrate that undesirable silylation of surface hydroxyl groups can be minimized by a pretreatment with Sb(NMe 2 ) 3 . The near‐saturation of nucleation sites on a metal oxide surface is demonstrated by scanning transmission electron microscopy and X‐ray reflectometry. Density functional theory highlights the importance of thermodynamics for surface inhibition and reactivation. The insight gained is applied to establishing a Sb 2 Se 3 ALD process which delivers smooth, continuous, ultrathin (<50 nm) films even after thermal annealing and crystallization. Such films are successfully incorporated into functional solar cells. Unraveling the details of nucleation chemistry for the specific case of Sb 2 Se 3 ALD also provides a perspective on adjusting chemical bonding at the interface between an oxide and a heavier chalcogenide.

10.1002/adfm.78748.abstract: NaNO 3 -DMSO reorganizes the local ion-association environment of a carbonate electrolyte by coupling Na + with PF 6 − while retaining reducible nitrate near the reaction interface. This dual-ion chemistry directs SEI formation toward a uniform LiF/NaF–N-rich interphase, enabling rapid Li + transport, suppressed side reactions, and durable cycling of Si/C anodes. ABSTRACT Silicon-carbon anodes offer high capacity for lithium-ion batteries, yet their cycling stability is limited by repeated solid-electrolyte-interphase (SEI) rupture during drastic volume changes. Herein, we introduce a NaNO 3 -DMSO additive into a conventional LiPF 6 /carbonate electrolyte to construct a durable LiF/NaF–N-rich interphase on a porous silicon-carbon composite (Si@pSC) through a dual-ion cooperative mechanism. We reveal that DMSO enables NaNO 3 incorporation while preserving the carbonate-rich Li + primary solvation sheath, with Na + strongly associating with PF 6 − and NO 3 − undergoing early interfacial reduction to seed nitrogen-containing inorganic species. This dual-ion synergy reconstructs the conventional carbonate-containing SEI by incorporating LiF/NaF nanocrystalline domains and nitrate-derived N-containing species, thereby limiting persistent parasitic interfacial reactions while providing accelerated Li + transport pathways. Consequently, the optimized electrolyte enables Si@pSC half-cells to deliver 365 mAh g −1 after 1000 cycles at 1 A g −1 , LFP||Si@pSC full cells retain 85.6% capacity after 1000 cycles at 2 C, and NCM811||Si@pSC full cells retain 95.4% capacity after 500 cycles at 2 C. Theoretical calculations further reveal that Na incorporation expands the fluoride lattice framework and lowers the Li + migration barrier from 0.56 to 0.42 eV. This dual-ion interphase reconstruction strategy offers a practical pathway toward durable Si-based anodes.

10.1002/adfm.78759.abstract: A graphene-supported 2D metal–organic network stabilizes highly reactive Fe(I)-N 4 single sites through Co-induced charge redistribution. Combined experiments and theory reveal Fe(I) formation, oxygen-driven oxidation, and O 2 activation mechanisms, offering a strategy to access low-valent iron centers relevant to catalytic and biological processes. ABSTRACT Stabilization of low-valent iron centers in atomically defined coordination environments remains a major challenge in the design of reactive metal–organic materials. Here, we report the rational stabilization of Fe(I)-N 4 single sites in a graphene-supported, two-dimensional metal–organic network assembled from FeTPyP tectons and Co coordination nodes. We find that nitrogen tetra-coordination in this specific bidimensional metal–organic network allows the stabilization of iron in the +1 oxidation state. Using state-of-the-art experimental techniques, complemented by theoretical calculations, we reveal that Co coordination induces charge redistribution across the network and reduces the porphyrinic Fe center from Fe(II) toward Fe(I). The latter species is highly reactive: even in ultra-high vacuum, residual oxygen-containing species oxidize the Fe center. O 2 activation occurs instead at near-ambient pressure, yielding the common Fe(II) species, as supported by dedicated theoretical models. These results demonstrate a coordination-network strategy to stabilize Fe(I) centers, which are believed to play a relevant role in a number of key reactions, including the biological synthesis of ammonia from N 2 .

10.1002/adfm.78809.abstract: This work presents a dual-field-driven strategy integrating a localized thermal field and a built-in electric field within a photothermal heterostructure. Cu single atoms anchored on CeO 2 /Co 3 O 4 promote NO 3 − adsorption and effectively inhibit the hydrogen evolution reaction. The dual-field facilitates the interfacial charge transfer and enhances the reaction rate, achieving efficient nitrate electroreduction to ammonia. ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic reactions involving multiple electrons and protons, such as nitrate reduction to ammonia, are constrained by sluggish interfacial charge-transfer and inefficient mass transport. Here, we propose a dual-field-driven strategy that integrates the local thermal field and the built-in electric field within a photothermal heterostructure, enabling concerted control over both atomic-scale active-site construction and the reaction microenvironment. Using a CeO 2 /Co 3 O 4 composite as the platform, photogenerated electrons guided by interfacial band alignment drive the site-selective loading of single-atom Cu onto CeO 2 domains, yielding an atomically precise Cu/CeO 2 /Co 3 O 4 (Cu/CeCo) catalyst. Under near-infrared irradiation, the optimal catalyst provides an NH 3 yield rate of 110.5 µmol h −1 cm −2 at −0.4 V vs. RHE and a high Faradaic efficiency of 95.8% at −0.2 V vs. RHE, both outperforming its dark-state performance. Mechanistic studies indicate that Cu single atoms anchored on CeO 2 /Co 3 O 4 promote NO 3 − adsorption and effectively inhibit the hydrogen evolution reaction. Furthermore, the dual-field accelerates the interfacial charge transfer and promotes the overall reaction kinetics. This work demonstrates that dual-field microenvironment engineering serves as a promising platform for advancing atomic-scale catalysis toward sustainable chemical synthesis.

10.1002/adfm.78813.abstract: Sulfur-regulated Sn@SnO x interfaces enable durable cyclohexanone oxime electrosynthesis through dual interfacial modulation. Cathodic potential-driven sulfur leaching buffers interfacial •OH, suppressing SnO x overgrowth and maintaining dynamically stable Sn@SnO x interfaces. Residual sulfur promotes water activation and *H generation, accelerating NO 2 − hydrogenation to NH 2 OH and subsequent oximation with cyclohexanone. ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic oxime synthesis from NO x and carbonyl compounds offers a sustainable alternative to conventional routes but remains limited by poor *NH 2 OH control and catalyst instability. Herein, we report a sulfur-decorated Sn@SnO x dendritic catalyst for efficient cyclohexanone oxime electrosynthesis from nitrite and cyclohexanone. Under operating conditions, the catalyst undergoes an adaptive reconstruction, where the cathodic potential-driven sulfur leaching triggers a buffered hydroxyl radical (•OH) microenvironment and suppresses •OH-mediated SnO x overgrowth, preserving dynamically stable Sn@SnO x interfaces. Meanwhile, residual sulfur could modulate the Sn@SnO x electronic structure, promoting water activation and *H generation to accelerate NO 2 − hydrogenation toward the key *NH 2 OH intermediate for subsequent oximation. At −1.0 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode, the reconstructed catalyst achieves an optimal Faradaic efficiency of 84.4%, with a yield of 87.1% and a yeild rate of 1.48 mmol h −1 cm −2 . This work establishes sulfur-mediated interfacial regulation as an effective strategy to reconcile activity and durability in Sn-based catalysts for NO x -to-oxime conversion.

10.1002/adfm.78831.abstract: This work reports a Co-NO/C catalyst featuring Co 3 O 4 and Co 4 N sites that synergistically activate nitrate for electrocatalytic reduction to ammonia (NH 3 ). Co 3 O 4 sites adsorb and activate NO 3 − , while Co 4 N sites provide active hydrogen (H * ). The system achieves high NH 3 selectivity and efficiency, demonstrating scalable nitrate remediation and ammonia recovery in a Zn–NO 3 − battery and MEA reactor. ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (eNO 3 RA) represents an emerging strategy for coupling nitrate remediation with nitrogen recovery and value-added ammonia production, but it remains challenging to simultaneously promote nitrate activation and downstream hydrogenation. Herein, we report a Co -NO/C catalyst featuring Co 3 O 4 /Co 4 N tandem catalysis sites embedded in a conductive carbon matrix. Structural and spectroscopic analyses suggest that Co 3 O 4 sites mainly favor nitrate adsorption/activation, whereas Co 4 N sites facilitate interfacial active-hydrogen generation. In an H-type cell, Co-NO/C delivers high NH 3 selectivity over a broad potential window and reaches a Faradaic efficiency of 99.7% at −0.6 V vs. RHE, with an NH 3 yield rate of 62.4 mg h −1 mg cat. −1 . Online differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS), 15 N isotopic labeling, in situ attenuated total reflection Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and spatially resolved scanning vibrating probe (SVP) measurements collectively support a stepwise nitrate-to-ammonia pathway involving sequential adsorption, deoxygenation, and hydrogenation of NO x -derived intermediates. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations further indicate spontaneous nitrate adsorption on Co 3 O 4 and favorable H * formation on Co 4 N sites. Device demonstrations in Zn–NO 3 − batteries and a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) reactor further suggest the practical promise of this tandem-site design for eNO 3 RA.

10.1002/adfm.79405.abstract: Dual FeCo and FeNi alloy nanoparticles are exsolved from a multi-doped Fe-based perovskite anode for high-performance direct ammonia solid oxide fuel cells. The dual-alloy surface coordinates electronic structure modulation and nanoparticle morphology control, providing abundant reaction sites and complementary catalytic functions for NH 3 decomposition, NH x dehydrogenation, and N 2 removal. Consequently, the R-LSBMFCN anode delivers efficient NH 3 utilization, suppressed anode polarization, and stable direct ammonia solid oxide fuel cell operation. ABSTRACT Direct ammonia solid oxide fuel cells (DA-SOFCs) offer an integrated route for carbon-free power generation by coupling in situ ammonia decomposition with electrochemical hydrogen oxidation. However, anode catalysts must simultaneously achieve rapid NH 3 decomposition, efficient electrochemical charge transfer, and long-term resistance to nitridation and particle coarsening. Here, we report an Fe-based perovskite multi-doped with Co and Ni, La 0.6 Sr 0.2 Ba 0.2 Mn 0.2 Fe 0.6 Co 0.1 Ni 0.1 O 3 (P-LSBMFCN), as a precursor for dual-alloy exsolved DA-SOFC anodes. Upon H 2 reduction, P-LSBMFCN transforms into a Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) layered oxide decorated with highly dispersed FeCo and FeNi alloy nanoparticles (R-LSBMFCN). Co and Ni multi-doping directs the reduction-induced nucleation and alloying pathway, reducing the average nanoparticle size from 129.3 nm for the Fe-only reference to 48.3 nm for R-LSBMFCN while increasing nanoparticle density. The resulting dual-alloy architecture provides abundant accessible active sites and electronically tuned metal surfaces, accelerating NH 3 activation, NH x intermediate conversion, and N recombination/desorption. Consequently, R-LSBMFCN exhibits the lowest apparent activation energy, nearly complete NH 3 conversion at high temperature, and maximum power densities of 1.638 and 1.386 W cm −2 under H 2 and NH 3 at 800°C, respectively, with stable operation for 200 h under NH 3 . This work demonstrates multi-doping-induced dual-alloy exsolution as an effective strategy for durable DA-SOFC anodes.

10.1002/adfm.79457.abstract: Precursor-domain size is identified as a decisive kinetic parameter in the solid-state synthesis of Na 4 Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 P 2 O 7 . Oversized Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 domains restrict Na/P penetration and retain unreacted cores, whereas intermediate domains undergo heterogeneous conversion with residual phases. Submicrometre domains shorten the required transport distance, enabling near-complete conversion and formation of a uniform redox-active NFPP framework. ABSTRACT Na 4 Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 P 2 O 7 is an attractive Fe-based polyanionic cathode for low-cost sodium-ion batteries, but scalable synthesis remains constrained by the trade-off between precursor homogeneity and process compatibility. Soluble Fe salts enable intimate mixing, whereas Fe (II)-phosphate precursors avoid nitrate/oxalate burdens but react as insoluble domains. Here we identify precursor defined solid state reaction length as the key variable governing NFPP formation from Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 . Reaction–diffusion simulations predict that oversized Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 domains retain under converted interiors, while low submicrometre domains enter a conversion-saturated regime. Experiments using size-controlled precursors confirm that this length scale regulates competing NaFePO 4 and Na 2 FeP 2 O 7 formation, Fe 2+ /Fe 3+ local chemistry and Na + transport kinetics. A CV precursor captures most of the kinetic and electrochemical benefit of stronger refinement, delivering 104.1 mAh g −1 at 0.1 C and 61.8 mAh g −1 at 20 C, together with stable long-term and full-cell operation. These findings establish reaction length scale control as a practical design rule for phosphate compatible NFPP synthesis.

10.1002/adfm.79467.abstract: The following paper sets out the design, synthesis, and schematic illustration of the photocatalytic nitrogen fixation mechanism of FeMnMOF photocatalysts with single-atom Mn─N sites. Among the prepared catalysts, U-FeMnMOF demonstrated the most effective photocatalytic nitrogen fixation capacity, with an ammonia yield of 1823.1 µmol·g −1 ·h −1 . ABSTRACT Photocatalytic nitrogen reduction involves complex proton-coupled multi-electron transfer processes, which bring about abundant reaction pathways and thus result in poorly controllable product selectivity. Benefiting from their unique electronic configuration and unsaturated coordination environment, single-atom photocatalysts can effectively regulate the reaction pathways of photoreductive N 2 activation and reduction, thereby improving the selectivity and NH 3 productivity of target ammonia products. Herein, an acetate-modified ultrasonication method is developed to construct atomically dispersed, coordinatively unsaturated Mn–N sites on Fe-based metal–organic frameworks (FeMOFs). Distinct from traditional carbon-based single-atom catalysts, these Mn─N sites are fabricated via a mild wet-chemistry approach without high-temperature treatment. The optimized U-FeMnMOF(Fe:Mn = 1:3) achieves a high NH 3 productivity of 1823.1 µmol·g −1 ·h −1 , 21.2 times that of pure FeMOF. Characterizations and DFT results verify that Mn─N sites not only activate N 2 and optimize hydrogen adsorption, but also work as a charge transfer mediator to form a direct Z-scheme heterojunction. This study presents a feasible strategy to synthesize non-carbon M─N single-atom catalysts for efficient PNRR.

10.1002/adma.75146.abstract: This work reduces the high energy consumption of electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia by coupling the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) with the nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR). The electrocatalyst design introduces P vacancies into CoP to form an atomic-scale electric field, which enhances the activity and selectivity of both HzOR and NO 3 RR, thereby ensuring a high ammonia yield. ABSTRACT Electrochemical nitrate-to-ammonia conversion holds great promise for sustainable nitrogen fixation, yet its industrial‑level current density operation is limited by cathodic active hydrogen (*H) supply shortage and high energy consumption caused by anodic oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Here, we develop a bifunctional CoP electrocatalyst with engineered phosphorus vacancies that generate atomic-scale electric fields to enrich interfacial water molecules via enhanced hydrogen-bonding interactions, alleviating local water scarcity caused by double-layer compression under high nitrate concentrations and promoting *H generation for nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR). Meanwhile, we replace OER with the thermodynamically favorable hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR), and the electrocatalyst promotes *OH adsorption to facilitate hydrazine dehydrogenation in HzOR. The resulting NO 3 RR||HzOR electrolyzer delivers an ammonia yield of 49.64 mg h −1 cm −2 at 500 mA cm −2 with a cell voltage of 0.962 V, and enables self-powered ammonia production at 0.769 g L −1 h −1 without external energy input. This work reveals atomic-scale electric field engineering as an effective strategy to modulate interfacial microenvironment for high-performance, low-energy ammonia electrosynthesis.

10.1002/adsc.70858.abstract: Photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia holds dual significance for nitrogen‐containing wastewater remediation and green ammonia synthesis. However, single‐component semiconductor photocatalysts are generally hampered by severe photogenerated charge recombination, insufficient spectral response, and poor substrate activation. Herein, cobalt porphyrin (CoTCPP) was in situ anchored onto the surface of Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 nanorods via a solvothermal method to construct CoTCPP/Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 photocatalysts featuring strong interfacial coupling. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis reveals a distinct interfacial electronic coupling between CoTCPP and Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 . This strong interfacial coupling synergistically enhances photocatalytic performance by facilitating rapid capture and efficient interfacial transfer of photogenerated electrons to effectively suppress charge carrier recombination, significantly broadening the near‐infrared (NIR) light response range, and strengthening the electrostatic adsorption of NO 3 − on the catalyst surface to accelerate the selective generation of NH 3 . The optimized 1.5CoTCPP/Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 achieved an NH 3 production rate of 1230.81 μmol·g −1 ·h −1 , approximately 5‐fold higher than that of pristine Bi 19 S 27 Br 3 . In situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed the stepwise deoxygenation–hydrogenation reduction pathway of NO 3 − → *NO 3 → *NO 2 → *NO → *NHOH → *NH 2 OH → NH 3 . This work provides an effective strategy for constructing interfacially coupled photocatalytic systems toward efficient nitrate reduction to ammonia.

10.1002/aenm.71764.abstract: Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is among the most promising techniques to provide hydrogen as both energy carrier and feedstock for the chemical industry, due to its compatibility with intermittent renewable electricity sources. However, a major bottleneck in scaling up PEMWE is the limited supply of the anode catalyst Ir. This work shows a novel approach to tailoring ionomer-free catalyst layers based on custom-made microporous substrates and two different atomic layer deposition (ALD) processes, both using Ir(EtCp)(CHD) precursor. Thermal ALD using O3 as counter-reactant yields mostly metallic Ir/IrOx and an electrode Ir loading of 0.21 mg/cm2. The PEMWE cell-level performance is comparable to a commercial catalyst-coated membrane anode despite 7x lower loading, and is maintained over an accelerated durability test equivalent to 600 h of intermittent operation. Moreover, using a low-loading ALD-made cathode, the total platinum group metal loading is only 0.24 mg/cm2. Plasma-enhanced ALD reduces the Ir loading to 0.04 mg/cm2 by tailoring the catalyst distribution, however, yields lower-activity IrO2. Finally, direct ALD catalyst deposition needs no ionomer-bearing ink. The anodes are therefore compatible with various membrane materials, as demonstrated in a CO2 electrolysis experiment with an anion exchange membrane.

10.1002/aenm.71791.abstract: Light irradiation dynamically generates oxygen vacancies at Ni/CeO 2 interfaces, forming Ce–Ov–Ni motifs that promote NH 3 adsorption and N–H activation while directing hydrogen intermediates to Ni sites. Vacancy-induced electronic modulation weakens H 2 adsorption, accelerates hydrogen release, mitigates hydrogen poisoning, and enables efficient low-temperature photothermal NH 3 -to-H 2 conversion. ABSTRACT NH 3 is an attractive hydrogen carrier, but efficient H 2 release is hindered by N–H bond cleavage and hydrogen poisoning. Herein, we develop Ni nanoparticle-supported CeO 2 (Ni/CeO 2 ) for low-temperature photothermal NH 3 decomposition. Light irradiation is accompanied by the dynamic generation of oxygen vacancies on CeO 2 , which couple with adjacent Ni sites to form Ce–Ov–Ni motifs, indicating that illumination can regulate the catalyst surface state beyond its thermal contribution. Experiments and DFT calculations indicate that these interfaces create differentiated local environments for NH 3 activation and product evolution. Oxygen-vacancy-associated sites favor NH 3 adsorption, N–H bond activation, and N-containing intermediates, whereas adjacent Ni sites accommodate H migration and recombination. Moreover, vacancy-induced electronic modulation weakens H 2 adsorption on Ni, thereby facilitating H 2 release. Such site differentiation and facilitated hydrogen removal reduce the competitive occupation of active sites by N- and H-containing species and contribute to the resistance to hydrogen poisoning. Under photothermal conditions, 10 wt.% Ni/CeO 2 achieves 96.3% NH 3 conversion at 450°C, versus 42.5% under thermal catalysis, and maintains >95% conversion at a GHSV of 18,000 mL·gcat −1 ·h −1 . It delivers 20.09 mmol·gcat −1 ·min −1 H 2 with 50 h stability. This work demonstrates light-induced oxygen-vacancy–metal interfaces for efficient, hydrogen-poisoning-resistant NH 3 -to-H 2 conversion.
10.1002/aenm.71791.title: Light‐Induced Ce–Ov–Ni Motifs Enable Hydrogen‐Poisoning‐Resistant Photothermal NH3 Decomposition

10.1002/aenm.71797.abstract: Phase-separated Janus CuCo alloys enable relay catalysis for electrochemical nitrate reduction at industrially low concentrations. Cu-rich and Co-rich domains play complementary roles, promoting nitrate activation, intermediate transfer, and hydrogenation at the Cu–Co interface. This interfacial synergy delivers enhanced activity, selectivity, and mechanistic insight for efficient nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. ABSTRACT Earth-abundant Cu and Co are attractive electrocatalysts for nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO 3 − RR); however, conventional solid-solution alloys with single-phase active sites lack effective intermediate spillover, impeding the hydrogenation of multiple reaction intermediates and limiting NH 3 selectivity under dilute nitrate conditions. Here we report phase-separated yet electronically coupled Janus–CuCo alloys synthesized via a time–charge regulated electrochemical reduction strategy, forming metallic Cu/Co domains with a well-defined interphase electronic structure. This Janus architecture enables relay catalysis, in which Cu domains activate NO 3 − , intermediates migrate to Cu−Co interfaces for hydrogenation, and adjacent Co domains promote subsequent NH 3 formation. In situ characterizations reveal pronounced Cu–Co synergy, where Co sites regulate *H-mediated hydrogenation while the balanced surface coverage of *H and *NO 3 − optimizes NH 3 selectivity and yield. Consequently, the optimized Janus Cu−Co catalyst, Janus–Cu 70 Co 30 /NOMC, achieves a peak NH 3 Faradaic efficiency (FE NH3 ) of 95.5% at −500 mA cm −2 and delivers a FE NH3 of 93.1% with an NH 3 yield rate of 4.2 mg h −1 mg cat −1 at −0.4 V vs RHE in an MEA flow cell under low nitrate concentrations. These findings establish phase separation with electronic coupling, enabled by electrochemical time–charge control, as an effective design principle for efficient multistep NO 3 − RR electrocatalysis.

10.1002/aenm.71803.abstract: ABSTRACT The performance and lifetime of energy‐storage devices are determined at the interfaces between electrodes, electrolytes, and separators, where ion and charge transfer, parasitic reactions, and mechanical degradation originate within nanometers of the surface. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) and molecular layer deposition (MLD) enable precise engineering of these interfaces through self‐limiting surface reactions that produce conformal coatings with controlled thickness and composition, even on porous electrodes. Although ALD surface chemistry is well established on ideal oxide surfaces, energy‐storage materials present chemically and structurally complex surfaces, on which reaction mechanisms, growth per cycle, and coating function can differ. This Review develops a chemistry–process–structure–function framework that connects surface chemistry, precursor reaction pathways, and nucleation behavior with film structure, ionic transport, charge‐transfer kinetics, redox stability, and mechanical response. We examine growth on oxide, sulfide, metal, polymer, and carbon substrates and relate the films to their functions at cathodes, anodes, solid electrolytes, and separators in Li‐based and beyond‐Li batteries. We further assess process scalability in terms of precursor utilization, throughput, and energy consumption, and discuss in situ monitoring, post‐deposition characterization, and full‐cell test conditions needed to validate coating performance. These relationships are summarized as six design rules presented as a decision flow.

10.1002/anie.1880547.abstract: ABSTRACT Continuous lithium‐mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li‐NRR), which integrates anodic hydrogen oxidation with cathodic nitrogen fixation, opens a viable pathway for ambient ammonia synthesis. Nevertheless, its long‐term and efficient operation remains tremendously challenging due to severe solvent issues including polymerization, volatilization, and reductive decomposition. Here, we fundamentally uncover the intrinsic reductive decomposition mechanism of solvent molecules in ion–solvent complex‐dominated electrolytes, and develop a weak‐solvent modulation strategy to significantly enhance the reduction stability of solvent frameworks toward durable and efficient Li‐NRR operation. The optimized weakly solvating electrolyte attenuates solvent molecule distortion by Li + and promotes the formation of an anion‑enriched solvation sheath and a nanocrystalline LiF‑rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Such a functional SEI layer effectively suppresses solvent decomposition on the cathode and constructs a fast Li + transport network via abundant surface pathways and grain boundaries, which synergistically improves Li plating kinetics and nitrogen fixation efficiency, as well as stability. Benefiting from these optimizations, we achieve stable and continuous N 2 electroreduction over 300 h. Meanwhile, the system delivers a high NH 3 Faradaic efficiency of 69.5% and an improved energy efficiency up to 23.2%. This work provides an effective molecular design strategy that significantly enhances the energy efficiency and stability of Li‐NRR.

10.1002/anie.2045143.abstract: Porphyrin–polyimide COFs enable one-pot oxygen reduction coupled ammoximation of cyclic ketones. Photoinduced electron transfer activates O 2 at imide carbonyl sites, generating *OOH that directly oxidizes NH 4 + to NH 2 OH, which then condenses with ketones. IMCOF-1 delivers cyclohexanone oxime at 18.55 mmol g − 1 h − 1 , avoiding H 2 O 2 accumulation and enabling a single-COF cascade. ABSTRACT Photocatalytic oxygen reduction over covalent organic frameworks (COFs) has been extensively studied for H 2 O 2 production, but the in situ utilization of oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) intermediates in chemical synthesis remains underexplored. Herein, two porphyrin-based polyimide COFs, IMCOF-1 and IMCOF-2, are reported as photocatalysts for the one-pot ORR-coupled ammoximation of cyclic ketones using O 2 and NH 4 OAc. Under light irradiation, IMCOF-1 achieves a cyclohexanone oxime formation rate of 18.55 mmol g −1 h −1 and is effective for several other cyclic ketones. Mechanistic investigations reveal that photoinduced electron transfer from the porphyrin units to the electron-deficient imide moieties promotes charge separation and activates O 2 at the carbonyl sites. The resulting surface-bound *OOH intermediates are proposed to participate in ammonia oxidation and subsequent NH 2 OH formation, which then condenses with cyclic ketones to yield the corresponding oximes. In contrast to stepwise systems that first accumulate H 2 O 2 before ammoximation, the present one-pot strategy enables the in situ utilization of oxygen-derived reactive intermediates without requiring substantial bulk H 2 O 2 pre-accumulation, eliminating the need for H 2 O 2 isolation, storage, and transport, thereby improving safety and atom economy while maintaining high selectivity. This work demonstrates the potential of directly harnessing ORR-derived intermediates for the light-driven synthesis of value-added nitrogen-containing chemicals.

10.1002/anie.2196422.abstract: An electron bridge strategy is developed to regulate charge polarization in Pd 1 and Ni 1 dual single-atom sites, promoting CO 2 reduction, nitrate reduction, and C–N coupling simultaneously. The resulting catalyst achieves efficient urea electrosynthesis with high activity and record durability over 1700 h. ABSTRACT Urea electrosynthesis from carbon dioxide and nitrates powered by green electricity is a zero-carbon route for urea production. Simultaneously achieving high activity and long-term stability is a prerequisite for the industrialization of urea electrosynthesis. In this study, we propose an electron bridge strategy based on a Pd 1 and Ni 1 dual single-atom alloy to boost the electrocatalytic activity and durability for urea electrosynthesis. The single-atom Ni 1 sites act as electron bridges to promote charge transfer from Cu to Pd 1 sites, leading to charge-polarized Pd–Cu sites, which upshift the d-band center and improve oxidation resistance of the catalyst. Consequently, the Pd 1 and Ni 1 dual single-atom sites simultaneously accelerates both carbon dioxide reduction and nitrates reduction half-reactions, while facilitating the first C–N coupling step. The Pd 1 and Ni 1 dual single-atom alloys deliver a urea yield rate of 541.6 mmol g cat −1 h −1 with a urea Faradaic efficiency of 57.3%. Remarkably, this catalyst achieves a record durability of 1700 h at a current density of 40 mA cm −2 . This work provides new insights into the synergistic catalysis of complex multi-molecule reactions through cooperative multiple active sites.

10.1002/anie.3751410.abstract: Nitro functional group was incorporated into NiFe-MOF ligands near metal sites, which undergo a simple and direct oxidation to NO 3 − and subsequently anchored on the reconstructed γ-NiFeOOH phase. The anchored NO 3 − not only forms a robust Cl − -repelling interface but also activates lattice oxygen to drive the efficient lattice-oxygen-mediated pathway for active and durable seawater electrolysis. ABSTRACT Chloride ions (Cl − )-induced corrosion severely limits the practical implementation of direct seawater electrolysis. Although oxyanion incorporation can mitigate Cl − poisoning, existing approaches offer limited control over oxyanion generation and retention during catalyst reconstruction. Herein, we report a MOF-based ligand-engineering strategy that enables defined oxyanion incorporation into reconstructed metal oxyhydroxides for active and durable seawater electrolysis. Nitro- (NO 2 ) functionalized ligands are incorporated into a NiFe-MOF precursor, where the NO 2 group undergo a simple and direct oxidation to nitrate (NO 3 − ) during electrochemical reconstruction, enabling well-defined NO 3 − regulation of the reconstructed γ-NiFeOOH phase. The anchored NO 3 − not only forms a robust Cl − -repelling interface but also activates lattice oxygen to drive a mechanistic transition from an adsorbate evolution mechanism to a more efficient lattice-oxygen-mediated pathway. The designed catalyst achieves excellent oxygen evolution reaction performance in alkaline seawater, requiring an overpotential of only 230 mV to reach a current density of 500 mA cm −2 , outperforming its NO 3 − -free counterpart. It also exhibits high durability, operating for over 4000 h at 1.5 A cm −2 with an ultralow degradation rate of 1.8 µV h −1 . Furthermore, a kilowatt-level alkaline seawater electrolyzer equipped with the designed electrode operates stably for over 1100 h under industrially relevant conditions.

10.1002/anie.4875918.abstract: Magnetically induced reactive carbon capture (RCC) was demonstrated for the first time with ferromagnetic multifunction materials (MFMs) capable of adsorbing CO 2 and converting it to methane via rapid temperature swing powered by magnetic induction heating. These MFMs exhibited no activity under conventional heating, establishing magnetic reduction as a key enabling step. Application of induction heating to RCC can dramatically improve productivity by shortening cycle time and establishing a new power-to-X paradigm. ABSTRACT Thermochemical reactive carbon capture (tRCC) offers a direct pathway to convert dilute CO 2 into valuable fuels and chemicals. However, the scalability of tRCC is hindered by the thermal inertia of conventional reactors, which limits reactor throughput. Here, we report the first demonstration of magnetically induced reactive carbon capture (mRCC), utilizing high-frequency alternating magnetic fields to drive rapid heating (200–400°C/min) of alkali-impregnated ferromagnetic catalysts. Operating as multi-function materials (MFMs), these sorbent–catalysts achieve high temperatures in minutes rather than hours, capturing and selectively converting dilute CO 2 into methane. Surprisingly, the optimal Na/NiFe exhibited stable CH 4 productivity under mRCC but was rendered inactive under equivalent conventional heating. Utilizing a novel magnetically programmed reduction (MPR) technique alongside in situ DRIFTS and STEM-EELS, we reveal that contact heating under reducing conditions drives phase segregation and alkali migration, eliminating the material's CO 2 capture capability. In contrast, localized magnetic heating preserves the functionality of the alkali capture sites while creating a reactive surface hydrogen pool. These findings show that magnetic induction does not merely accelerate heating but fundamentally alters the local catalyst–sorbent environment. Ultimately, this work establishes critical design principles for induction-heated catalysis and advances mRCC as a scalable power-to-X strategy for rapid carbon valorization.

10.1002/anie.7471326.abstract: Embedding hydrazone photoswitches into hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks enables sequential, programmable macroscopic optical outputs. Ammonia exposure unlocks solid-state E / Z photoisomerization, which triggers a cascade reorganization of TPE packing to modulate coloration and luminescence, providing a design paradigm for high-security, information-dense smart photofunctional materials. ABSTRACT Light-driven molecular switches enable precise and noninvasive regulation of molecular structure and function, and thus represent fundamental building blocks for stimuli-responsive photofunctional materials. However, translating molecular-level photoswitching into sequence-dependent macroscopic outputs in the solid state remains a formidable challenge. In this study, we report a supramolecular strategy that integrates guanyl hydrazone switches into hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) to overcome this limitation. A tetrasulfonate-substituted tetraphenylethylene anion ( TPE 4 − ) is employed as the host scaffold, while guanyl hydrazone ( G2 ) functions as the photoresponsive guest, affording a functional framework through cooperative assembly. This system leverages a reversible crystalline–amorphous phase transformation, triggered by acid–base stimuli, to gate the solid-state photoisomerization of G2 . Upon activation, the configurational switching of G2 induces a cascade reorganization of the TPE 4 − packing motifs, leading to pronounced and sequence-dependent modulation of both fluorescence and macroscopic coloration. In addition, the applicability of this system in information encryption has been demonstrated. This work expands the design paradigm of hydrazone-based photoswitches in the solid state and provides a supramolecular strategy for constructing intelligent optical materials with high information density and enhanced security.

10.1002/anie.9224223.abstract: First electrocatalytic synthesis of hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) via paired electrolysis: A bifunctional Fe–Ni 2 P catalyst concurrently reduces nitrate to ammonia (∼96.0% FE) and oxidizes ethylene glycol to formaldehyde intermediates, coupling them into HMTA with ∼75.2% carbon selectivity. ABSTRACT Hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) is a critical organonitrogen compound widely used in the defense, pharmaceutical, and polymer industries. Conventional HMTA production relies on toxic formaldehyde (HCHO) and energy-intensive Haber–Bosch-derived ammonia (NH 3 ) as feedstocks. This study demonstrates a sustainable electrocatalytic approach for the direct synthesis of HMTA via paired electrolysis, using nitrate (NO 3 − ) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste as nitrogen and carbon sources, respectively. With iron-doped nickel phosphide (Fe–Ni 2 P) as a bifunctional catalyst, the system achieves concurrent cathodic NO 3 − reduction to NH 3 with a Faradaic efficiency of ∼ 96.0%, and anodic oxidation of PET-derived ethylene glycol to electrophilic *HCHO intermediates. These resulting intermediates subsequently condense with nucleophilic NH 3 to form HMTA with ∼75.2% carbon selectivity. Mechanistic studies reveal that Fe doping induces charge redistribution and upshifts the d-band center, thereby facilitating the adsorption and activation of reactants and lowering the energy barrier for *HCHO intermediate formation and desorption—a critical step enabling subsequent C─N coupling. This work establishes a mild and sustainable electrocatalytic route for HMTA synthesis from environmental waste, underscoring the potential of paired electrolysis in valorizing waste into valuable organonitrogen chemicals.

10.1002/cctc.71144.abstract: ABSTRACT Nitric oxide (NO), a major atmospheric pollutant emitted from fossil‐fuel combustion and industrial processes, poses serious risks to both ecosystems and human health. At the same time, ammonia (NH 3 ) is an essential chemical feedstock and energy carrier, although its conventional production relies on energy‐intensive Haber–Bosch synthesis. Compared with nitrogen reduction, nitric oxide reduction reaction (NORR) benefits from the intrinsic reactivity and higher solubility of NO molecules. However, achieving efficient and selective NO‐to‐NH 3 conversion remains challenging due to complex reaction pathways, competitive hydrogen evolution, and limited NO availability under ppm‐scale dilute feeds relevant to practical environments. In this review, we provide an overview of recent progress in NORR, covering mechanistic understanding, catalyst design, electrolyte engineering, and reactor optimization. Particular attention is given to strategies for regulating the interfacial microenvironment and improving performance under environmentally relevant ppm‐scale NO conditions. Finally, we discuss the major obstacles that still hinder practical implementation and outline future directions for developing efficient and scalable NORR systems for realistic NO remediation and sustainable NH 3 electrosynthesis.

The hydrolysis of ammonia borane (NH 3 BH 3 , AB) under mild reaction conditions was assessed in this work using a highly active Ru–Ni alloy catalyst supported on CeO 2 . As‐synthesized Ru–Ni/CeO 2 with different metal contents was used as a heterogeneous catalyst for the mild hydrolytic dehydrogenation of AB. At 298 K, the optimal catalyst is Ru 0.5 Ni 1.25 /CeO 2 , which demonstrated exceptional catalytic activity with a TOF value of 1226.0 mol H2 min − 1 . The calculated apparent activation energy was 37.5 kJ mol −1 , which is even lower than that of the majority of noble‐metal‐based catalysts for AB dehydrogenation. Strong electronic interactions and synergistic effects between Ru and Ni led to the formation of a bimetallic alloy structure with increased catalytic activity when Ni was incorporated into Ru. The dispersion and stability of the nanoparticles were enhanced by CeO 2 ’s strong metal–support interactions, and high oxygen storage capacity, which made it an efficient support. Additionally, after several catalytic cycles, the catalyst showed exceptional structural stability with little activity loss. This study demonstrates the potential of Ru–Ni/CeO 2 as an economical and effective catalyst for applications involving the production of hydrogen.

10.1002/cphc.70624.abstract: Electrochemical reduction of nitric oxide (NO) to ammonia (NH 3 ) integrates pollutant abatement with green chemical synthesis. Using density functional theory with the computational hydrogen electrode model, we investigate NO electroreduction on a boron‐doped GeS 2 monolayer (B@S‐GeS 2 ) containing complementary Ge and B active centers. At the Ge site, the distal pathway operates as the minimum‐energy pathway under gas‐ and aqueous‐phase conditions, achieving a barrier‐free limiting potential ( U L = 0 V vs. RHE) driven by early N─O bond cleavage following double O‐end protonation. Conversely, the electron‐deficient B site exhibits stronger NO binding ( E ads = −2.14 eV). Although strong postcleavage N stabilization yields U L = −0.218 V, implicit solvation stabilizes polar intermediates, establishing a near‐degenerate dual‐pathway mechanism (Δ U L = 0.027 V). Both sites intrinsically suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction via severe H overbinding (Δ G H = −0.93 to −1.57 eV) and competitive NO adsorption. Additionally, competing N 2 O/N 2 formation pathways are kinetically and thermodynamically disfavored (Δ G PDS = +0.61 to +2.19 eV). Outperforming benchmark 2D catalysts, B@S‐GeS 2 presents a highly selective, dual‐site platform for ambient NO‐to‐NH 3 valorization.

10.1002/cssc.71193.abstract: LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) cathode material has attracted considerable attention because of its potential to achieve substantially higher energy densities, but the practical deployment of NCM811 remains hindered by severe interfacial and structural degradation during repeated cycling. By constructing a stable and ionically conductive interfacial protective layer, the LSO coating achieves the synergistic optimization of interfacial stability, structural stability, and electrochemical kinetics, thereby markedly enhancing the electrochemical performance of NCM811 cathode materials. This work provides important insights into interfacial engineering design for high‐nickel layered cathode materials of lithium‐ion batteries.

10.1002/elt2.70075.abstract: ABSTRACT The photochemical reduction of nitrogen offers an environmentally friendly approach for ammonia synthesis, providing an alternative to the energy‐intensive and emission‐heavy Haber–Bosch process. Despite its promise, the process is impeded by slow nitrogen activation and excessive hydrogen evolution. To overcome these limitations, we present a tandem nickel phthalocyanine (NiPc)/CNT‐P&Cu‐BCN photocatalyst, engineered with an organic–organic heterojunction for enhanced nitrogen conversion. This system integrates boron‐doped (B), nitrogen‐deficient (N) carbon nitride (CN), modified via Cu–Cu coordination and phosphorus doping through sodium borohydride‐assisted thermal treatment, with hydrogen‐bonded, ultrathin NiPc nanosheets. This novel design yields a record ammonia production rate of 915.4 μmol g −1 h −1 under visible light, a remarkable 16‐fold increase compared to traditional BCN materials. The improvement is attributed to precise bandgap engineering; boron doping and nitrogen vacancies adjust the electronic structure, while the synergistic effects of Cu, P, and CNT enhance charge transfer dynamics. The ultrathin NiPc framework introduces atomically dispersed active sites, whereas a Z‐scheme‐driven charge separation mechanism facilitates efficient electron movement. This work, by integrating defect engineering, heterojunction design, and single‐atom catalysis, contributes to the advancement of photocatalytic nitrogen fixation, offering a scalable pathway for sustainable ammonia production. The results underscore the importance of multi‐component synergy in overcoming kinetic barriers, opening new avenues for energy‐efficient alternatives to conventional synthesis methods.

10.1002/smll.76525.abstract: ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction enables sustainable ammonia production and simultaneous nitrate pollutant abatement. Yet its multi‐step proton‐coupled electron transfer mechanism is hindered by slow reaction kinetics. Herein, we report a reconstructed tandem catalyst, Fe‐MOFs@Cu, generated through the in situ electrochemical transformation of a designed MIL‐101(Fe)@HKUST‐1 core–shell precursor. Under nitrate reduction conditions, the HKUST‐1 shell is selectively converted into Cu species, whereas the MIL‐101(Fe) core remains largely preserved, resulting in a reconstructed Cu/Fe heterointerface with spatially integrated active domains. Electrochemical and kinetic analyses reveal a clear functional differentiation between the two catalytic components. Cu‐rich domains preferentially promote nitrate activation to nitrite, while Fe‐based sites facilitate water activation and the subsequent hydrogenation of nitrite to ammonia. The close interfacial coupling between these domains enables efficient intermediate conversion and hydrogen utilization, thereby suppressing nitrite accumulation and competing hydrogen evolution. Benefiting from this cooperative catalytic architecture, R‐MIL‐101(Fe)@Cu achieves an NH 3 yield rate of 0.61 mmol h −1 cm −2 with a Faradaic efficiency of 94.9% at −0.5 V vs. RHE, together with excellent operational stability. This work demonstrates how precursor architecture can be deliberately engineered to direct electrochemical reconstruction toward catalytically favorable interfaces for complex multistep electrochemical transformations.

10.1002/smtd.71203.abstract: ABSTRACT The electrochemical synthesis of ammonia through nitrogen reduction (ENRR) is hindered by N 2 inertness and competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Phosphorene, despite its promise, inherently lacks the eletron‐backdonation capability for effective N 2 activation. Herein, we present a water‐free hydrogen bubble electroetching strategy to simultaneously exfoliate and engineer black phosphorus into defect‐rich porous phosphorene (D‐BP ene ) with abundant in‐plane phosphorus vacancies for ENRR catalysis. Four‐dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy resolves distorted hexagonal rings where pairs of P atoms from the upper and lower sub‐layers show mutually perpendicular orientations. D‐BP ene exhibits superior electrocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction performance, achieving a high NH 3 yield of 14.94 µg h −1 mg cat −1 at −0.05 V versus RHE and a Faradaic efficiency of 35.51% at 0 V versus RHE that corresponds to an ultralow overpotential of 92 mV, outperforming most metal‐free catalysts, while remaining stable for over 36 h. Density functional theory calculations reveal that phosphorus vacancies act as Lewis acid sites, reducing the energy barrier for the potential‐determining step from 2.012 to 1.387 eV via strengthened σ‐donation and π‐backdonation, while increasing the HER kinetic barrier by inhibiting *H desorption. This work presents an effective synthetic route to vacancy‐engineered two‐dimensional materials with potential applications extending beyond nitrogen fixation.

10.1007/s40820-026-02359-6.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO 3 − RR) offers a route to couple wastewater remediation with green ammonia (NH 3 ) synthesis, but remains kinetically and mechanistically challenging under high-current-density operation. Herein, an N-doped carbon-encapsulated NiCo alloy catalyst (NiCo@NC) is derived from a NiCo-ZB precursor supported on conductive carbon black. The cathodic NO 3 − RR over NiCo@NC achieves an NH 3 yield rate of 187 mol h −1 g cat −1 with 95% Faradaic efficiency (FE) at −0.6 V RHE in an H-type cell and sustains ~92% FE at 2.0 A cm −2 under a cell voltage of 3.3 V in a membrane–electrode assembly. Pairing this cathodic NO 3 − RR with anodic methanol oxidation to formate enables simultaneous NH 3 and formate production at 2.1 A cm −2 under a cell voltage of 2.8 V, while maintaining NH 3 and formate FEs above 90% and 96%, respectively. In situ Fourier transform infrared and operando X-ray absorption fine structure spectra reveal preferential *NO stabilization and reversible Co valence/coordination, while theoretical calculations disclose interfacial charge polarization between NiCo alloy core and N-doped carbon shell, fabricating dual sites, comprising electron-deficient graphitic carbon and electron-rich pyridinic-N domains, that accelerate water dissociation/proton supply and lower the barrier of the rate-determining *NO → *NOH step. 10.1016/j.apcatb.2026.127755.abstract: Ammonia adsorption-desorption plays a pivotal role in plasma-catalytic ammonia synthesis, yet the influence of catalyst acidity on regulating this dynamic process remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the effect of zeolite acidity on plasma-catalytic NH 3 synthesis by systematically tuning the acid-site distribution of zeolite 4 A through cation exchange. Among the catalysts examined, Ni/Ca-4A achieved an NH 3 synthesis rate of 8858.2 μmol g -1 h -1 at a specific energy input (SEI) of 12 kJ L -1 and an N 2 /H 2 ratio of 2:1, more than ten times higher than that of unmodified zeolite 4 A. Comprehensive catalyst characterization, plasma diagnostics and in situ NH 3 monitoring reveal that catalyst performance is governed by the dynamic adsorption-desorption behavior of NH 3 under plasma conditions. Ca-exchanged 4 A possesses a high concentration of plasma-accessible acid sites, defined as acid sites with NH 3 desorption temperatures within the local reaction temperature range (~210-275 o C) measured in the discharge region during plasma-catalytic ammonia synthesis, enabling transient NH 3 storage and controlled release. This dynamic process enhances NH 3 formation while mitigating plasma induced NH 3 decomposition. In contrast, unmodified 4 A is dominated by stronger acid sites that retain NH 3 excessively, hindering desorption and limiting catalytic activity, particularly at low specific energy inputs. Furthermore, Ni promotes H 2 activation, while plasma-accessible acid sites continuously regulate NH 3 storage and release, resulting in a synergistic enhancement of ammonia synthesis performance. Within the investigated zeolite catalyst series, the concentration and distribution of plasma-accessible acid sites serve as a useful descriptor for understanding NH 3 adsorption–desorption dynamics and catalytic performance under the investigated plasma conditions, providing mechanistic insights to guide the rational design of efficient catalysts for plasma-catalytic ammonia synthesis.

10.1016/j.apsusc.2026.168935.abstract: The reduction of nitric oxide (NO) is a powerful method for eliminating the pollutant NO and a feasible route for synthesizing ammonia (NH 3 ) at ambient temperature, a promise to replace the energy-consuming Haber-Bosch process. However, the design of efficient catalysts with low cost and high activity to boost the complex electron transfer process is significantly challenging. Herein, we applied state-of-the-art density functional theory (DFT) calculations for the first time to investigate NO reduction on black-phosphorus-like two-dimensional monochalcogenides GeSe and SnSe, respectively. The strong bonding state between the catalyst and the adsorbate is attributed to the activation of NO, favouring NO-side adsorption and the substantial reduction to NH 3 . The catalysts are highly efficient for nitric oxide reduction reaction (NORR), as evidenced by the low limiting potentials of −0.19 and −0.11 V, respectively. Moreover, the formation of by-products (N 2 O and N 2 ) and the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) are strongly suppressed, indicating the selective formation of NH 3 . This work is a promising strategy for designing practical and economical NORR electrocatalysts and an effective method to solve the problem of NO environmental pollution.

10.1016/j.aqrep.2026.103903.abstract: Isochrysis zhanjiangensis is crucial in the breeding of bivalves larval as an artificially cultivated feed microalga. To investigate their roles in algal–bacterial interactions, we isolated and identified two phycospheric bacterial strains, Halomonas piezotolerans and Alteromonas abrolhosensis, from I. zhanjiangensis and examined their effects on algal growth and ammonia nitrogen removal in aquaculture systems. The results indicated that both bacterial strains promoted the growth of I. zhanjiangensis; however, the effect of A. abrolhosensis was more pronounced. At a concentration of 108 cfu/mL, the A. abrolhosensis treatment group reached a cell density of 1.082 × 107 cells/mL on day 10, significantly higher than the control group by 16.26% (p 0.05). Furthermore, H. piezotolerans enhanced soluble protein synthesis at low concentrations. In ammonia nitrogen removal experiments, H. piezotolerans showed superior and stable activity, while A. abrolhosensis also promoted nitrogen reduction. The qPCR validation revealed upregulation of nirB and nosZ genes in H. piezotolerans, and enhanced expression of nirB, glnG, glnL, and glnA genes in A. abrolhosensis, confirming their ammonia nitrogen removal potential. This study demonstrates that phycospheric bacteria isolated from I. zhanjiangensis promote algal growth and facilitate ammonia nitrogen removal during bivalves larval rearing. These results provide new insights into bacteria–algae interactions and indicate practical implications for enhancing algal productivity and maintaining environmental stability in hatchery systems.

10.1016/j.cej.2026.183530.abstract: Conventional ammonia synthesis relies on steam methane reforming (SMR) to produce hydrogen while concurrently supplying high-purity nitrogen as a by-product for the Haber-Bosch process. However, the shift to green ammonia, where hydrogen is produced via electrolysis, eliminates this nitrogen source, necessitating an energy-efficient air separation unit (ASU) to prevent catalyst poisoning from O 2 impurities below 10 ppm. Pressure swing adsorption units face prohibitive energy penalties when targeting such ultra-low impurities, as energy demand escalates exponentially below 1 vol% O 2 . To overcome this scalability barrier, we demonstrate a thermochemical redox cycle using SrFeO 3 (SFO) integrated with ASU pre-purification for the first time. Our 6.5 kg packed-bed reactor achieves 450 °C restricts purity to ≥ 2 ppm due to thermodynamic limitations. A purified nitrogen flow of up to 0.35 kg/s per kg SrFeO 3 was achieved. This work provides the first reactor-scale validation of a scalable, energy-efficient nitrogen supply for green ammonia, addressing a key bottleneck in decarbonizing fertilizer and energy sectors.

10.1016/j.ecmx.2026.102431.abstract: The potential of various metal oxides as redox carrier materials was investigated for on-demand hydrogen/ammonia production and solid-state storage through solar chemical-looping processes. Metal production involves solar-driven reduction assisted by various bio-sourced reductants, while nitride synthesis requires a similar reduction process supplemented by nitrogen incorporation. The reduced metals act as long-term solid storage media. Steam oxidation of metals (or nitrides) produces pure H 2 (or NH 3 ). A selection of oxide/metal and oxide/nitride pairs was carried out to identify the most promising systems. Suitable metals were screened according to multi-criteria: thermodynamic feasibility/conversion extents at equilibrium, cycle/process efficiencies, energy/exergy demands, specific storage density, and material availability/cost. Mo, W, and V offer high volumetric H 2 storage density despite low abundance and high cost. Al, Si, Mg, Fe, Mn, Cr, and Ti balance favorable storage performance with high availability and affordability, making them adapted for large-scale H 2 storage, while Zn, Sn, Ga, Ge, Ca, Sr, Ta, and Sc are less abundant or show moderate performance, suited mainly for niche uses. Regarding nitrides for NH 3 synthesis, AlN, TaN, ZrN, W 2 N, TiN, and Ge 3 N 4 formation from oxides with C/N 2 was thermodynamically feasible. Furthermore, energy and exergy analysis revealed that Fe(s), Mo(s), Sn(s), W(s) systems show maximum solar-to-fuel efficiencies (40–50% for C, 20–25% for CH 4 reductant), followed by Ga(g), Ge(s), Mn(g), V(g), Zn(g), Ta(s), and B(s). They also require the lowest exergy demand and inversion temperatures. In contrast, Al(g), Ca(g), Cr(g), Mg(g), Si(g), Sr(g), Ti(g), and Sc(s) show lower process efficiencies and higher exergy requirements due to higher temperatures and associated losses. The cycle temperatures could however be decreased in open reactor systems or by tuning the operating conditions to favor metals synthesis.

10.1016/j.egyr.2026.109890.abstract: Green hydrogen and green ammonia supply chains integrate variable renewable electricity with electrolysis, nitrogen separation, ammonia synthesis, storage, transportation, reconversion, and end-use decisions. However, the optimization literature remains heterogeneous in mathematical assumptions, system boundaries, temporal representation, uncertainty treatment, adaptive decision mechanisms, and computational tractability, limiting consistent model selection and cross-study comparison. This paper presents a systematic and critical review of optimization models for integrated green hydrogen and ammonia supply chains, based on 118 studies. The review applies a controlled record-level taxonomy covering the base modeling or assessment approach, objective structure, dominant supply-chain scope, spatial scale, temporal structure, time-step resolution, uncertainty treatment, and adaptive or online mechanism. The result indicates a concentration in recent publications, regional applications, deterministic formulations, and production-oriented models. Linear and network-planning approaches, particularly mixed-integer linear programming, dominate strategic infrastructure and capacity decisions, whereas full-chain integration, dedicated storage and conversion modeling, formal stochastic and robust uncertainty treatments, and adaptive or online decision mechanisms remain underdeveloped. Building on this synthesis, the review develops a decision-oriented model-selection framework, technology-to-model matrices, uncertainty-propagation and industrial-feasibility assessments, a harmonized comparison of direct hydrogen, direct ammonia, and ammonia-to-hydrogen pathways, and a gap-to-method roadmap. Future research should prioritize hybrid multi-scale architectures integrating strategic network planning, validated nonlinear or surrogate process models, stochastic or robust optimization, decomposition, rolling-horizon control, digital twins, and lifecycle, safety, resilience, and sustainability metrics. The resulting framework supports scalable, uncertainty-aware, and industrially credible supply-chain models for integrated green hydrogen and ammonia systems.

10.1016/j.fub.2026.100225.abstract: Ammonia-mediated energy storage system offers a promising approach to bridging intermittent renewable electricity generation and dispatchable power supply through an integrated electricity–ammonia–electricity cycle. In this system, renewable electricity is first converted into ammonia via power-to-ammonia (P2A) conversion, stored and transported as a chemical energy carrier, and then reconverted into electricity via ammonia-to-power (A2P) technologies. This review discusses the ammonia-mediated energy storage system from an electrochemical perspective, covering both P2A and A2P conversions. For P2A, renewable hydrogen-assisted Haber–Bosch synthesis is considered the most technologically mature route for practical deployment, while emerging electrochemical nitrogen and nitrate reduction pathways are examined in terms of their potential and limitations. For A2P, indirect configurations coupling ammonia cracking with hydrogen fuel cells are compared with ammonia-fed solid oxide fuel cells (NH₃-SOFCs) and anion exchange membrane direct ammonia fuel cells (AEM-DAFCs). The current progress, technical barriers, and system-level implications of these routes for renewable electricity conversion and storage are analyzed. We conclude that ammonia-mediated energy storage is unlikely to rely on a single technology pathway. Instead, its practical deployment will depend on continued advances in both P2A and A2P technologies, followed by system optimization for efficient, durable, and dispatchable renewable electricity storage.

10.1016/j.ijhydene.2026.158547.abstract: Ruthenium (Ru) catalysts exhibit high activity for ammonia (NH 3 ) synthesis and decomposition, governed by promoter chemistry, catalyst structure, and metal–support interactions (MSI). This review presents a descriptor-guided framework linking electronic, geometric, interfacial, and dynamic properties to reaction mechanisms and catalytic performance. Key steps, including nitrogen (N 2 ) dissociation, hydrogenation, nitrogen recombination, and hydrogen (H 2 ) inhibition, are examined alongside support selection, particle-size control, morphology, and interfacial engineering. Alkali, alkaline-earth, and rare-earth promoters are evaluated for their effects on Ru electronic structure, adsorption energetics, and active-site accessibility. Oxygen vacancies (OVs), strong metal–support interactions (SMSI), and electronic metal–support interactions (EMSI) are discussed as regulators of interfacial reactivity. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing mechanistic descriptors from experimental proxies and accounting for their coupling under reaction conditions. Finally, machine learning (ML) approaches are assessed for identifying transferable descriptors and guiding rational Ru catalyst design.

10.1016/j.isci.2026.118154.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) offers a promising approach to produce ammonia (NH3) under ambient conditions. However, the ammonia yield rate and Faradaic efficiency were still limited by the chemical inertness of nitrogen. Here, we report the introduction of Se vacancies in CoSe nanorods via an ions-exchange method. Se vacancies can improve the NRR activities by the lending of N2 activation. As a result, the ammonia yield rate reached as high as 106.7 μg h–1 mg–1 with a Faradaic efficiency of 21.2% at -0.3 V (vs. RHE). More importantly, the ammonia is directly derived from nitrogen, which was demonstrated by the isotopic experiments using 15N2 as a nitrogen source. This work not only provides a strategy for creating Se vacancies, but also offers an important pathway for the development of efficient catalysts for NRR. Ammonia (NH3) golds significant importance as carbon-free energy carrier, and industrial feedstock.[1-3] Currently, industrial-scale NH₃ is produced via the highly energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process, which operates under elevated temperatures (400–600°C) and high pressures (200-400 atm). However, this process emits substantial quantities of greenhouse gases, giving rise to significant environmental concerns. To achieve carbon neutrality, the Haber-Bosch method must be transformed into a low-carbon process. Powered by renewable energy sources, such as solar cells, the electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) under ambient conditions offers a promising route toward sustainable NH₃ production.[4-9] Despite the numerous NRR catalysts reported to date, the Faradaic efficiency and ammonia yield of NRR remain relatively low due to the inherent chemical inertness of N₂ molecule.[8-12] Vacancy engineering is widely acknowledged in the literature as an effective strategy for enhancing the catalytic activity of electrocatalysts.[13-17] For instance, Qiu et al. demonstrated that introducing oxygen vacancies into OER and ORR catalyst significantly improves its catalytic performance,[18] while Qiao et al. enhanced the catalyst's capability to activate and adsorb nitrogen molecules by incorporating nitrogen vacancies into nitrides.[19] Nevertheless, research on vacancy engineering specifically for NRR remains limited. Investigating the impact of vacancies of different elements on NRR performance could provide crucial insights for the design of highly efficient catalysts. In this work, we report a highly twinned CoSe nanorod with a large density of Se vacancies (denoted as V-CoSe) via an two-steps ion-exchange method, which exhibits significantly superior Faradaic efficiency and NH3 production rate. The theoretical calculations suggest that the Se vacancies are essential for NRR of V-CoSe, which greatly promote the adsorption and activation of N2. This work provide a new strategy to introduce vacancies into catalysts for green and sustainable NH3 production. Ion exchange is a particularly attractive synthetic tool for adjusting the atomic/electronic structure of electrocatalysts. Herein, V-CoSe nanorods with atomic steps were prepared via the two-steps ion-exchange method. First, CoO nanorods were fabricated using single-crystal ZnO nanorods as sacrificial templates. After cation-exchange, ZnO nanorods were completely transformed into CoO nanorods. Second, V-CoSe nanorods were synthetized using CoO nanorods as sacrificial templates (Fig. S1). After cation-exchange, CoO nanorods were completely transformed into V-CoSe nanorods (Fig.1a). As shown in Fig. S4, large-area, uniform growth of CoSe on the carbon fibers is evident. Compared to the smooth surfaces of the ZnO (Fig.S2), CoO (Fig.S3) and pristine CoSe (Fig. S5) nanorods, the V-CoSe nanorods exhibit significantly rougher surfaces. TEM and high-resolution imaging (Fig 1b,c) reveal that the CoSe nanorods synthesized via ion exchange possess abundant twin boundaries and atomic steps. This structure can be primarily attributed to the rearrangement of atoms within the crystal lattice during the anion exchange process.[20] Fig. 1e shows the Three-dimensional (3D) reconstructions images of V-CoSe from two-dimensional (2D) high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (Fig. 1d), which clearly reveals the surface of V-CoSe nanorod is full of cavities, which should be caused by the release of crystal stress during the anion exchange process. These cavities can significantly enhance the mass diffusion during NRR. The XRD patterns (Fig. 2a) and TEM-EDS results (Table S1) demonstrate CoO were completely converted into V-CoSe after cation exchange. Both the V-CoSe nanorods and pristine CoSe nanorods exhibit the hexagonal phase structure (PDF card No.89-2004).

10.1016/j.jcis.2026.141853.abstract: Photocatalytic N 2 fixation is a promising route for sustainable ammonia (NH 3 ) synthesis. Its efficiency depends on light absorption, charge separation, and active sites. Hydrogen tungsten bronze (H x WO 3 ; HWO) exhibits distinct advantages for nitrogen (N 2 ) fixation owing to its broad ultraviolet-visible-near-infrared light absorption and abundant oxygen vacancies. Nevertheless, the structural instability originating from the extraction of lattice hydrogen during catalysis severely restricts its practical applicability. Herein, we report the design of a hydrogen extraction and insertion dynamic ruthenium (Ru)-supported HWO (Ru/HWO) system for stable and efficient photocatalytic N 2 fixation. During the reaction, the release of lattice hydrogen from HWO accelerates the N 2 reduction reaction. Active hydrogen species are generated at the water-dissociation sites on Ru spillover to HWO, replenishing lattice hydrogen and establishing an efficient, dynamic hydrogen cycle. Benefiting from this unique mechanism, a remarkable NH 3 yield of 228.5 μmol g -1 h -1 is achieved, with full-spectrum light use extending from the ultraviolet to the infrared region. We propose a lattice hydrogen-mediated photocatalytic pathway for N 2 reduction, paving the way for rational design of efficient, stable HWO photocatalytic systems.

10.1016/j.jcis.2026.141916.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction (NO₃RR) offers a promising route for ammonia synthesis, but is hindered by slow kinetics and competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Herein, ultrathin Cu‐doped Co₃O₄/reduced graphene oxide (Cu‐Co₃O₄/rGO) nanosheets are prepared through the morphology and electronic structure modulation for efficient NO₃RR performance. Combined experiments and DFT computations disclose that Cu doping induces 2D nanosheet morphology, up-modulates the d‐band center to optimize the adsorption strengthen of reactants and key intermediates, and constructs Cu‐Co tandem sites for cascade catalysis, while rGO improves the composite conductivity. The optimized catalyst exhibits a Faradaic efficiency of 98.5% at -0.7 V vs. RHE and an ammonia yield of 25.2 mg h-¹ mgcat-¹ at -1.0 V vs. RHE with high stability. The in‐situ electro‐generated ammonia acts directly as a base catalyst for chalcone synthesis with 75.9% conversion, constructing a waste‐to‐resource‐to‐value model integrating nitrate remediation and sustainable fine‐chemical synthesis.

10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.131297.abstract: With cumulative spent lithium-ion battery (LIB) waste projected to exceed 11 million tonnes by 2030, rapid and low-carbon regeneration technologies are increasingly important for securing secondary resources. Joule heating provides heating and cooling rates of 103-105 K s-1 and millisecond-to-second thermal exposure, enabling impurity removal, lattice reconstruction and non-equilibrium defect regulation while limiting prolonged diffusion and side reactions. This review critically synthesizes Joule heating-enabled recycling, regeneration and upcycling of spent LIB anodes and cathodes, together with the underlying mechanisms, industrial barriers and environmental implications. Representative graphite-regeneration studies report >99% removal of Li and transition metal contaminants using only 0.1 M HCl, with regenerated or upcycled graphite delivering approximately 351-459 mAh·g-1. For cathodes, Joule heating direct regeneration restored spent LiCoO2 from 103.9 to 133 mAh·g-1 within 8 s. Quantitative TEA and LCA further indicate that representative graphite regeneration routes require approximately 1.05-15.38 MJ kg-1 and cost $1.48-5.79 kg-1, with greenhouse gas (GHG) reductions of up to 98% depending on the comparator and system boundary. Joule heating assisted cathode recycling has reported 72-82% lower GHG emissions than conventional benchmarks. However, most demonstrations remain at laboratory or gram scale. This review identifies spent graphite regeneration as the most immediately deployable field and cathode direct regeneration as a high-value but more feedstock-sensitive target, while emphasizing adaptive process control, transparent LCA/TEA boundaries and responsible scale-up as priorities for industrial translation.

10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.144152.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) represents a sustainable paradigm for simultaneous environmental remediation and green NH 3 production. While single-atom catalysts (SACs) exhibit immense promise for NO 3 RR, precisely manipulating their localized orbital interactions to decode the underlying structure-activity relationships remains a critical challenge. Herein, using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we designed a series of interlayer single-metal-atom coordinated porous boron nitride (IC-M/p-BN) acting as efficient electrocatalysts for NO 3 RR. Interlayer metal confinement triggers robust interfacial p-d-p orbital hybridization, establishing an efficient electron relay that empowers surface-exposed non-metallic B sites to act as direct catalytic centers while effectively suppressing the competing HER, NRR and toxic NO/NO 2 byproducts. Crucially, this interfacial charge transfer drives a dynamic B sp 2 -to-sp 3 reconfiguration, facilitating optimal NO 3 - activation. Benefiting from this mechanism, IC-Co/p-BN and IC-Ni/p-BN deliver outstanding NO 3 RR activity (limiting potentials of -0.51 and -0.50 V vs. RHE), significantly outperforming their conventional h-BN counterparts. Furthermore, machine learning analysis identifies the work function as the fundamental descriptor governing NO 3 - adsorption, revealing the interfacial catalytic mechanism. Our work not only offers a robust design strategy for high-efficiency 2D confined SACs but also provides deeper insights into the dynamic NO 3 - -to-NH 3 conversion mechanism at non-metallic interfaces.

10.1016/j.jiec.2026.11.006.abstract: Enhancing catalyst durability under continuous-flow operation remains a major limitation for the practical implementation of advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) in water treatment. In this work, pulsed magnetic induction heating (MIH) is proposed as a low-energy regeneration strategy for magnetically responsive fixed-bed reactors, enabling recovery of catalytic activity under continuous operation. A Fe 3 O 4 @PLA composite was employed as catalytic bed for persulfate activation and ofloxacin (OFX) degradation, showing high initial activity (up to 98 % removal at 40 °C) but undergoing progressive deactivation. A short MIH pulse enabled reactor regeneration, restoring degradation efficiencies up to 94 % and allowing sustained operation for up to 16 days, with stable OFX removal around 79 %. Post-use characterization revealed structural and compositional changes, including migration of Fe 3 O 4 towards the surface, increased PLA crystallinity, and partial Fe 3 O 4 oxidation. These results suggest that thermal effects and mass transport phenomena contribute to catalyst reactivation, while oxidation processes may limit complete recovery of catalytic activity. The system was also partially regenerated by MIH in real wastewater matrices, although significant matrix effects remained. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of pulsed MIH as a practical and energy-efficient regeneration strategy, enabling extended lifetime and stable operation of fixed-bed catalytic systems for continuous water treatment.

10.1016/j.proci.2026.106741.abstract: This study assesses the Incompletely Stirred Reactor Network (ISRN) approach in terms of accuracy in capturing the scalar distributions in an ammonia-fuelled staged combustor employing various degrees of NH 3 partial cracking, characterised by the molar ammonia decomposition ratio (DR). Underlying solutions from Large Eddy Simulation with Conditional Moment Closure (LES-CMC) with D R = 0.25 for 10 bar and D R = 0.50 for 5 bar are used to explore the behaviour of the combustor at varying D R at the range 0.1 < DR < 0.9 at constant pressure without repeating the CFD simulation. The basic hypothesis is that the mixing field does not change significantly as the fuel changes, which enables the exploration of parameter spaces with a single reference LES-CMC simulation. The ISRN model accurately predicts temperature and NOx distributions across the full range of D R tested, showing good agreement with both LES-CMC and experiment. The sensitivity to the chemical mechanism is also explored and it is found that NOx is predicted similarly from all schemes tested. The results suggest that ISRN can be used as a low-order model for ammonia combustor emissions, which facilitates the design process and provides insights to the flame structure as operating parameters change. Novelty and significance statement: This work demonstrates the first application of the combined framework of Large Eddy Simulation-Conditional Moment Closure (LES-CMC) with Incompletely Stirred Reactor Network (ISRN) modelling approach to predict NOx emission in an ammonia-fuelled laboratory-scale high pressure (10 bar) gas turbine combustor. ISRN is a computationally efficient, low-order model that incorporates detailed chemistry, mixture fraction spatial inhomogeneities, and chemistry evolution as a function of space. Using LES-CMC as a high-fidelity reference CFD solution, ISRN explores the operating parameter space, in this case, the NH 3 decomposition ratio at the fuel inlet, while maintaining agreement with experimental and LES-CMC predictions. The approach also allows a quick evaluation of the impact of the chemical mechanism used on NOx formation without having to repeat expensive CFD calculations.

10.1021/acs.est.6c07061.abstract: Abstract Land-based enhanced rock weathering (ERW)─applying ground silicate rock to soils─is being explored for sequestration of CO2 from the atmosphere, with impacts beyond carbon storage. Weathering of basalt releases base cations increasing alkalinity and soil pH, which we hypothesized would reduce N2O emissions. Repeated applications of basalt to a heavily fertilized annual Zea mays and Glycine max rotation (maize and soybean) and the low-fertilized perennial bioenergy grass Miscanthus x giganteus (miscanthus) in Illinois raised soil pH from 6.6 to 7.1 in maize/soybean and from 5.4 to 6.3 in miscanthus and consistently reduced annual N2O emissions by 16–40% over 7 growing seasons. Although not statistically significant for any given crop, our results indicate an emerging trend of increased N leaching (23% pooled across crops and years), suggesting a potential shift in N loss from the atmosphere to groundwater. Crop yields increased or remained unchanged, indicating enhanced weathering is compatible with conventional farming practices. Regional land model simulations show that ERW deployment across the US Corn Belt could reduce soil N2O emissions by 11% under a moderate deployment pathway and by 24% under a more intensive deployment pathway. The effects of enhanced weathering extend beyond CO2 sequestration and may benefit both greenhouse gas mitigation and bioenergy crop production, with a potential trade-off of increased N mobility in fertile, organic matter-rich US Midwestern soils.
